items.title: David N. Baker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Joe Wilder telling me of all the people, like Jimmy Owens said, who have no health insurance...

ctx.x: . . . that Ted McDaniel’s dad taught [at] that produced all those Memphis-ians – Memphis people such as James Williams and Mulgrew Miller and all those guys. So we are pioneers only because we are – by accident of birth happened to be in the place at the same time. But then you’ve got to certainly give a lot of credit to those pioneers who we don’t know. We don’t know about the people who never got their name in a book or never wrote a book, but prepared the way and laid the groundwork for what else was going to…

annihilate the whole classical system, where a clarinet player learns to play, studying with [Howard] Klug, and he plays like Klug until he gets his own voice. If he’s studying violin with [Josef] Gingold, he’ll play like Gingold until he gets his voice. People somehow or another don’t want jazz musicians to go through that. So I’ve always felt that it was imitation-assimilation-innovation; and until that idea somehow or another [is] planted in mind, I think we’re going to make mistakes. I got very tickled when…

items.title: 67848_Jimmy McPartland oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] Now of course Dave Baker is doing a good job out at Indiana University, teaching jazz.

ctx.x: Rhythms and the European melodic line and harmonies, the wedding of the two has really made American jazz in my opinion. And let's hope we can keep it that way and get married for ever. (LAUGHTER).
Now of course Dave Baker is doing a good job out at Indiana University, teaching jazz.
Oh fantastic. Well I just have a feeling this is a coming thing that all the colleges and schools will eventually get to include this in their curriculum.
